newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S. sanctions to hurt Japan shipping firms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sanctions to hurt Japan shipping firms.

text.p: The U.S. decision to slap surcharges on Japanese vessels calling at U.S. ports from April is expected to deal a severe blow to Japan's ailing shipping firms, industry sources and analysts said on Thursday.
"We are having a hard enough time without the U.S. sanctions," said a spokesman for Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha, one of the three shippers to be hurt by the move.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) said on Wednesday it would impose $100,000 surcharges on Japanese vessels calling at U.S. ports in retaliation for what it called "unfavourable restrictive practices".

The surcharges, effective from April 14, would be imposed each time a vessel owned or operated by Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd and Nippon Yusen KK enters a U.S. port from abroad, but not from another U.S. port, the FMC said.

The surcharges, to be imposed only on container carriers, would cost the three Japanese shipping firms a combined annual five billion yen ($41.3 million), Noboru Sakata, chairman of the Japan Shipowners' Port Council, told a news conference.

Japan's shipping industry has seen business shrink in recent years as the yen's surge against the dollar in 1995 hurt the competitiveness of Japanese exports and caused a rush by manufacturers to shift production overseas.
Even though the yen has weakened against the dollar since then, any positive factors from the reversal has been overtaken by low global freight rates for regular lines, analysts said.
Analysts doubted the sanctions, if they were to go into effect, would last for a year, but said company profits would be damaged.
"Regular lines are a loss-making business, losses will grow if the sanctions are imposed," said Jun Harada, an analyst with Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

Leading shipping firm Nippon Yusen has forecast current profits to total 16.50 billion yen ($136 million) in the 1996/97 year ending March, compared with 14.26 billion yen ($117 million) in the previous year. Current profit is pretax and includes gains or losses on non-operating activities such as investment in stocks.
The three shippers said they plan to bear the surcharge costs themselves and not pass on expenses to cargo holders.
Analysts noted that the sanctions would not only damage the business of Japanese shipping firms, but also affect some foreign shippers as well.
"Many shipping firms have alliances with overseas shipping firms to cooperate in cargo shipments," Yamaichi's Harada said.
Analysts said the U.S. threat to impose sanctions on Japanese shipping firms, which are not involved in deciding port practices, was unreasonable.
However, in the long-term, Japan's shipping industry would benefit from deregulation in port practices, they said.
Yasuhiro Shimizu, a senior economist with LTCB Research Institute said: "Japanese shipping firms are suffering the most from the port practices since they use Japanese ports the most."
